day1_consultation01.presenting_complaint: I've been having really bad diarrhea for the last 3 days
day1_consultation01.note:
Subjective: The patient reports diarrhea for three days with watery and loose stool, pain in lower abdomen on left side, weakness, shakiness, and a temperature of around 3-4 days ago. The patient also mentions vomiting that stopped, loss of appetite, and drinking fluids (soups, smoothies). The patient ate at a Chinese restaurant four days ago. No blood in stools or vomit. Patient is an accountant working at the moment. Lives with wife and two children. No smoking or alcohol use. Asthma controlled with inhaler. No other medications. Symptoms affecting daily activities due to frequent bowel movements. Patient feels it may be gastroenteritis, possibly caused by Chinese takeaway.
Objective: Diarrhea for 3 days, watery stool, lower abdominal pain on left side, weakness, shakiness, temperature of around 3-4 days ago, vomiting that stopped, loss of appetite, drinking fluids (soups, smoothies). No blood in stools or vomit. Asthma controlled with inhaler.
Assessment: Gastroenteritis possible, possibly caused by Chinese takeaway.
Plan: Conservative management: stay hydrated, electrolyte drinks, paracetamol for fever and weakness if needed, rest for 2-3 days if symptoms don't improve. Follow up in 3-4 days if symptoms persist to rule out other causes or consider stool sample testing.

day1_consultation02.note:

The patient has had eczema in the past and tried over-the-counter steroid cream which did not help. The patient also mentions using antihistamines without success. They have no bleeding or discharge from the skin. The patient is unsure of the cause of the symptoms but suspects it could be a flare-up of their eczema. The patient has been hiking recently, but nothing else that may trigger the rash. Patient reports being itchy and sore.
Objective: The patient has an itchy and sore skin rash on their chest, hands, and arms. The rash appears to be similar to their past eczema. The patient is using steroid cream from the pharmacy without success. They are also using antihistamines without success. No bleeding or discharge noted. Patient reports dry skin.
Assessment: Likely flare-up of eczema.
Plan: Prescribe stronger prescription steroid cream and emollients for use in bath and shower. Prescribe fexaphenidine as an antihistamine. Advise patient to keep a diary of potential triggers (e.g., soaps, clothing). Return in one week if symptoms do not improve. Suggestion: Diagnosis: Eczema flare-up. Rationale: Patient's history of eczema and the current presentation are consistent with a flare-up. Management: Prescribe stronger steroid cream and emollients for topical application. Suggestion: Diagnosis: Dry skin. Rationale: The patient reports dry skin, which can contribute to itching and irritation. Management: Recommend regular use of emollients in bath and shower. Suggestion: Diagnosis: Allergic reaction. Rationale: Patient is unsure of the cause of symptoms but suspects it could be a flare-up of their eczema. Management: Advise patient to keep a diary of potential triggers (e.g., soaps, clothing).

Plan: Keep a headache diary. Treat headaches with paracetamol/cocodamol and ibuprofen/naproxen. If symptoms worsen or new neurological deficits develop (neck pain, vision changes, weakness), return for evaluation immediately.
